p: Ken found two tables in Lumen's staging seed that had never been scrubbed, and Copilot had been reading them.
The folder had come over in Priya's July migration, marked already scrubbed. She said it was hers before anybody asked.
Ken fenced the folder off from Copilot, and the team learned where that fence doesn't reach, like agent mode in the editor.
Priya talked Joyce out of telling the board that Copilot couldn't see patient data anywhere. The true version had a folder in it.
By Friday the real rows were gone, replaced with invented ones, and Ken and Priya both signed that the fence held.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. He just installed Copilot in his terminal, and he's the one asking now.
Ken Ito. Security lead. The switches are his.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. He asks before he does things now, mostly.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. She owns the team's fixtures prompt now.
Tomasz Nowak. Leads Kraków. His people start work while Denver sleeps.
Nora Kim. Compliance. She wants every number traceable to its source.
Anders texted on Sunday night at 11:40, which for Anders was early. installed the copilot thing in my terminal. it says halcyon won't let me use it. fix that and I'll show you something.
Priya read it Monday at six with the kettle going and decided it was the nicest thing he'd said about Copilot since October.

The kettle clicked off at 6:30, and Asha's five photos came in right behind it. Across the top card, in purple: Week seven. Standing orders. The doctor can't be at every bed, so she writes down what you're allowed to do without calling her. Learn them on your first night, not your worst one.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: Seats. Finance wants to know why we're paying for Copilot seats nobody's using. The invoice and last week's usage report are about thirty people apart. The billing cycle closes with the month. Can I have a real list by Friday? Real meaning right, not short. Joyce
She drove in thinking about the word real, and about Anders, who had never once texted her to come see something.
Learn them on your first night.
Asha's first card said: A standing order lets a nurse act without paging the doctor. Read every one before your first shift. The night you need it is a bad night to find out what it says.

Under it Priya wrote what the GitHub docs say. GitHub Copilot CLI puts Copilot's agent in your terminal. It answers questions, writes and debugs code, edits files, runs commands, and works with GitHub.com: it can list your pull requests, open an issue, or create a pull request with you as the author. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, in PowerShell or WSL. The case for it is less context switching. Infrastructure work happens in a terminal, and you can ask about unfamiliar code right where you are.

It has two ways in. Type copilot for an interactive session, where you hold a conversation and steer the work. Pass -p or --prompt with a single prompt and it does the task and exits, which is how scripts use it. Inside a session, Shift+Tab moves between the default mode, plan mode, which asks questions and builds a plan before it writes any code, and autopilot, which keeps working without stopping to ask. To install it you need an active Copilot plan. With npm and Node 22 or later, run npm install -g @github/copilot. Homebrew uses brew install --cask copilot-cli, WinGet uses winget install GitHub.Copilot, and macOS and Linux also have an install script. The first time, it asks you to sign in with /login. For headless use, a fine grained personal access token from your personal account, with the Copilot Requests permission, works through an environment variable such as COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN. If your seat comes from an organization, the organization's Copilot CLI policy has to allow it. copilot help lists the options, and shows them inside a session. You may still see gh copilot suggest and gh copilot explain in older material. That was an earlier GitHub CLI extension, and it's been retired. Today's tool is the copilot command.

How the exam asks it. Know the install routes (npm's @github/copilot package, Homebrew, WinGet, the script), that it needs a Copilot plan, that an org seat needs the Copilot CLI policy, and interactive versus -p.
The second card: On nights you had your rooms. You didn't walk into somebody else's patient just because the door was open.

When you start the CLI, it asks whether you trust the files in and below that folder. You can trust it for this session, trust it and remember it, or say no and leave. Trusting it means Copilot may read, change, and run files there. So start it in the project you're working on. GitHub's advice is not to launch it from your home directory, from a folder with programs you can't vouch for, or from one holding sensitive files you don't want touched. Remembered folders sit in a list in the CLI's config file under your home directory.

By default the CLI can reach the working directory, the folders below it, and the system temp folder. It asks before it touches a path outside them. /add-dir adds another folder, and /cwd or /cd moves the session somewhere else. GitHub says these path checks are heuristic and don't guarantee that files outside are protected. --allow-all-paths turns path checks off. Websites need your approval by default too. Two policy facts from last week still apply here. Per GitHub's docs as of October 2026, the CLI respects content exclusion for Business and Enterprise users, though an older note said otherwise, so test it like any fence. The public code filter policy doesn't reach the CLI. And for Business and Enterprise, CLI prompts and suggestions are kept for 28 days.
How the exam asks it. Start the CLI in the project folder, not your home directory. Trusting a folder covers everything below it. Path checks are heuristic, so don't treat them as a wall.
The third card was underlined twice. A standing order names the drug, the dose, the route, and when. I never saw one that said use your judgment. That's what the phone call was for.

The first time Copilot wants a tool that can change or run files, like touch, chmod, node, or sed, it asks. Usually you get three choices: yes, once; yes, and approve that tool for the rest of the running session; or no, and tell Copilot what to do instead. The second choice approves the tool, not the command. GitHub's own example: approve rm ./this-file.txt that way, and Copilot can run any rm, rm -rf included, until the session ends. A new or resumed session asks again. Newer versions can also offer to remember an approval for this location, saved to a file in the CLI's config folder. That one lasts past the session, so treat it like trusting a folder.

Flags set this up ahead of time. --allow-tool lets one tool run without asking. --deny-tool blocks one, and a deny always beats an allow. A tool is named as shell(COMMAND), with a first level subcommand for git and gh, like shell(git push); as write, for file edits that aren't shell commands; or by an MCP server's name, with a tool in parentheses if you want just one. --allow-all-tools skips every tool prompt, and --allow-all, also called --yolo, drops the path and URL checks as well. GitHub warns that with all tools allowed, Copilot has your access to your files and can run any command you can, without asking. On Business and Enterprise, an enterprise administrator can block the allow all options. A programmatic run can't stop to ask, so it needs approval flags. Give it the fewest that work, and run anything broad in a sandbox (/sandbox enable), a container, or a virtual machine.

How the exam asks it. The session approval covers the whole tool, any arguments. Deny beats allow. Programmatic runs need approval flags, so keep them narrow and keep people on anything that changes state.
The fourth card: Report isn't the whole shift. It's what the next nurse needs, and nothing she doesn't.

CLI sessions are saved. copilot --continue picks up the most recent session in that folder, and --resume or /resume lets you choose one from a list, with its context. /clear or /new starts fresh for an unrelated task. Near the limit, the CLI compacts old history on its own. /compact does it whenever you ask, /context shows what's filling the window, and /usage shows the session's statistics. In the CLI, typing and a path adds that file to the prompt, as in explain @infra/main.tf. That's not IDE chat, where calls a participant and adds a file. Starting a line with runs a shell command without calling the model. /model switches models, /feedback sends GitHub a note, and /every, still an experimental command, repeats a prompt on a schedule while that session stays open.

For work you don't want to watch, /delegate, or a prompt that starts with hands the task to the cloud agent on GitHub. It offers to commit your unstaged changes to a new branch as a checkpoint, opens a draft pull request, works in the background, and asks you for a review. It only works if the organization allows both the Copilot CLI and the cloud agent. Autopilot is different: it stays on your machine. The CLI can also send a focused job to a built in subagent, like Explore for questions about the code or Task for builds and tests, which works in its own context so your main session stays clean. /agent lists custom agents, and a repository can add its own in .github/agents. The CLI reads the same instructions as everything else: .github/copilot-instructions.md, path specific instructions files, and AGENTS.md. It comes with the GitHub MCP server, and /mcp add adds more. /review runs a code review agent on your changes.
How the exam asks it. In the CLI, adds a file. --continue or --resume brings a session back; /clear starts fresh. /delegate goes to the cloud agent and a draft pull request; autopilot stays local.
The last card: Every shift started with a census. Who's here, who's leaving, and who's on the board but not in a bed.

Organization owners set Copilot policies in the organization's settings, under Copilot, then Policies. If an enterprise owner has already enabled or disabled a policy, the organization can't override it. People follow the policies of whoever gives them their Business or Enterprise seat. If two organizations in one enterprise disagree, the least restrictive setting usually wins, and GitHub lists the Copilot CLI and Copilot code review policies that way. Across different enterprises, the most restrictive usually wins. The CLI has its own policy, separate from the Copilot app. Turning on the Copilot code review policy is the first step, and rulesets can then request reviews automatically. Policy changes show up in the audit log, which is where to watch for drift.

Seats can be managed with the REST API, whose Copilot endpoints are in public preview. GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing returns the seat breakdown and policy settings, including whether the CLI is enabled. GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/seats lists every billed seat with last_activity_at and last_activity_editor, but activity in an IDE only shows up if that person's IDE telemetry is on. POST /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_users adds seats. DELETE on the same path sets them to pending cancellation: access ends at the end of the billing cycle, unless the person also gets a seat through a team, which the selected_teams endpoints manage. GET /orgs/{org}/members/{username}/copilot shows one person's seat. Only organization owners can manage seats. With a classic token, reading needs manage_billing:copilot or read:org, and changing seats needs manage_billing:copilot or admin:org.
How the exam asks it. Know the billing and seats endpoints, owners only, pending cancellation until the cycle ends, team seats surviving a user removal, and that activity depends on telemetry.

At nine Anders put his laptop on her desk, open to a terminal. He'd installed the CLI on Sunday night with one npm command, typed copilot, signed in, and been told politely that his organization didn't allow it.
Ken was already standing behind him. He'd seen the laptop cross the room.

I left the CLI policy off in October. On purpose. Nobody had asked for it, and I don't turn on what nobody's asked for. He looked at Anders. Somebody's asking. Before it goes on, I want to know what it can reach.
Anders installed Copilot for his terminal, and signing in says his organization doesn't allow it. What should Priya do?
A. Set every Copilot policy to enabled, the CLI and all previews included.
B. Have Ken check what the CLI reaches, then turn its org policy on.
C. Have Anders sign in with a personal access token instead of his account.
D. Reinstall the CLI through Homebrew in place of the npm package he used.

Ken opens GitHub's table of which policies reach which surfaces before he touches the switch. Content exclusion applies to the CLI, the docs say, and he says he'll test that the way they did last week. The public code filter doesn't reach it. Its prompts are kept for 28 days. Then he sets Copilot CLI to Enabled, and the change lands in the audit log under his name. Anders types copilot again. Now it wants to know if I trust my home directory. Do you? Not even slightly.

That's the one I'd sign. Org seats follow the organization's Copilot policies, and the CLI has its own. An organization owner enables it in the Copilot policies settings, unless the enterprise already decided. Read what a surface reaches before you open it.
By ten the CLI policy was on.

Anders had typed copilot from his home folder, which was where his terminal always opened. Everything he'd touched in seven years was under there somewhere: a folder called src with a dozen repos in it, his SSH keys, a folder called taxes.
The CLI wanted to know if he trusted all that. His cursor was already sitting on choice two, the one that says remember this folder.
The Terraform's in Lumen. The deploy scripts live in their own repo. I want it to see both, and I'm not starting it twice.
Anders opened the CLI in his home folder and is about to remember it. What should he do?
A. Trust the home folder for this session only and close it after.
B. Quit and restart it in the Lumen repo with /add-dir for the scripts.
C. Remember the home folder and let it reach every repo there from now on.
D. Start it again with --allow-all-paths and skip the folder question.

He presses Esc, changes into the Lumen repository, and starts it there. When the work needs the deploy scripts, he types /add-dir with that path. That's two folders. The keys, the taxes, and ten other repos never come into it. Home is where I keep everything, he says. That's the problem with it.

That's how I'd chart it. Whatever folder you trust, Copilot may read, change, and run files in it and everything under it. So the CLI belongs in the project folder, not home, which GitHub warns against by name. /add-dir brings in a second folder mid session.
At two Anders asked her to come watch.
In October it explained my Terraform in the editor and got one thing backwards, he said. Let's see what it does in a terminal.

He typed: explain the staging database module. Copilot answered about the wrong one. There were three staging database modules under infra/modules: staging-db, staging-db-old, and staging-db-v2, which nobody had finished. The one he meant was the oldest. He'd written it in 2019.
It had picked up the instructions file and his Terraform file on its own, rules and all. Wrong module anyway.
The CLI explained the wrong database module. How should Anders get the right one?
A. Type #file:main.tf into the prompt, the way he would in IDE chat.
B. Name the file with @infra/modules/staging-db/main.tf and ask again.
C. Copy the module out of his editor and paste all of it into the prompt.
D. Put @workspace at the front of the prompt to search all three modules.

He types explain, then an at sign and the path to the old module's main file, and Tab finishes the path for him. The answer walks the module from top to bottom: the instance, the backup window, prevent_destroy on the database. Then it quotes a comment he left in 2019 and forgot about. Don't shrink this below 100 GB, the restore needs room. He reads it twice. I wrote that for whoever came next. Something came next. He doesn't argue.

That's what I'd want on my shift. In Copilot CLI, plus a relative path, like @infra/modules/staging-db/main.tf, pulls that file into your prompt, and the path autocompletes. IDE chat flips it: is a participant there and is a file. The exam likes that swap.
Decision four. For the rest of the session.
By Tuesday morning Anders's desk had become a place people stood. Devin was there with coffee. Renata had brought a chair.
Anders had asked the CLI to clear out old plan files from the drift checks. It wanted to start with one.

The Copilot CLI in lumen, Tuesday at 9:12. Anders asked it to delete the plan files in infra plans older than 30 days, and it wants to run rm, the delete command, on the first one, a staging plan from September second. It offers three choices: one, yes; two, yes, and approve rm for the rest of the running session; three, no, and tell Copilot what to do differently.
There were forty one files. I'm asking, not telling. Two, right? Devin said. Otherwise you're pressing one all morning.
The CLI wants approval to delete an old plan file, the first of many. Which choice should Anders make?
A. Choose 3 and ask for a script that lists the files it would remove.
B. Choose 1 forty one times and read each file name before saying yes.
C. Choose 2 and approve rm for the rest of this running session.
D. Restart the session with --allow-all-tools and let it finish the job.

Anders presses Esc and asks for a script that lists plan files older than 30 days and deletes them only when given a --delete flag. It writes cleanup-plans.sh. He runs it without the flag and gets forty one names. The last is the plan for Thursday's change, copied from a backup on Friday with September's date. He fixes the check, runs it again, then runs it with --delete. Two would've taken Thursday's too. Two would've taken anything called rm.

That's the one I'd sign. Approving a command for the rest of the session approves the tool, not just that command. Say yes to rm that way once and Copilot can run any rm until the session ends. For bulk file work, have it write a script you can read and dry run first.
Tuesday at three Tomasz called with his camera on. It was eleven at night in Kraków, and he'd waited up for this.

My team starts at seven. Twice this month they found drift in staging at ten, after building on it. I want a drift check waiting for them every morning. Your Anders says the CLI can do anything now. Can it do this every morning?
Behind him, on Kraków's own whiteboard, someone had copied Denver's two columns, agent mode on the left and the coding agent on the right, coffee cup and all.
Tomasz wants a drift check waiting for Kraków every morning. How should the team build it?
A. Have the CLI write a drift script and put it through code review.
B. Use /every in a CLI session, left running, to check for drift.
C. Assign the cloud agent an issue asking for a drift check every morning.
D. Have each Kraków engineer log on and ask the CLI about drift.

Anders asks for a script that runs terraform plan with -detailed-exitcode in each workspace, prints one line per workspace, treats exit code 2 as drift, and never applies anything. It writes drift-check.sh in a minute. He reads every line, runs it against staging, and finds it skips a workspace with a space in its name. Copilot fixes the quoting. He opens a pull request, and Tomasz reviews it before he goes to bed. Good. A script does the same thing every morning. A prompt might get creative.

That's how I'd chart it. Copilot CLI is good at writing scripts. For a job that must run the same way every day, have it write one, then read, test, and review it like any other code. The script runs without a model, so it's the same every time.
Wednesday at ten Renata came to Priya's desk, because Anders was in a meeting and she'd decided not to wait.
She'd spent an hour in a CLI session in the Lumen repository, working through the infra folder module by module with Anders's checklist. Then her laptop had restarted for an update.
Is that hour just gone? I don't want to start over and explain it all again.
Renata's laptop restarted an hour into a CLI session in the Lumen repo. What should she do?
A. Ask the cloud agent for the session log it keeps of every chat.
B. Start a new session and type in what she remembers of the last hour.
C. Run copilot --continue in that folder to pick up where she left off.
D. Run /compact in a new session to pull the old session back in.

She types copilot --continue in the Lumen folder, and the hour comes back: her questions, the answers, the plan she'd started. It saved it? Sessions are saved. Continue takes the most recent one. Resume gives you a list. Renata names the session with /rename before she does anything else. Later she types /clear before an unrelated question, and Priya doesn't have to tell her why.

That's what I'd want on my shift. The CLI saves sessions. copilot --continue resumes the most recent one in that folder, and --resume or /resume lets you pick from a list, context included. Use /clear or /new between unrelated tasks.
Wednesday afternoon Anders was deep in the staging module, the old one, splitting it into pieces he could test. He had four terminals open and the look he got when he didn't want to be talked to.
Tomasz messaged anyway. Thirty modules, thirty READMEs, all wrong since the summer. My new people read them first. Can Copilot fix them without stopping you?
Under it Tomasz added: Our whiteboard has editor and GitHub. Where does the terminal go?
Kraków wants thirty module READMEs fixed while Anders keeps refactoring. How should that get done?
A. Hand the READMEs off with /delegate and review the pull request it opens.
B. Ask for them in his current session before he goes back to the refactor.
C. Use agent mode in VS Code and do the READMEs between refactor steps.
D. Run the READMEs in autopilot with --yolo and let it work through them.

Anders types /delegate update the README in each module to match its variables and outputs. The CLI offers to commit his unstaged work to a new branch as a checkpoint, then hands the task to the cloud agent. A link appears to a draft pull request and the agent's session. He goes back to the refactor. By five the pull request is waiting, thirty READMEs, two of them describing variables that don't exist. He mentions @copilot in a comment, and it fixes them. Terminal hands it to GitHub. I'll draw an arrow.

That's the one I'd sign. /delegate, or a prompt that starts with sends a task from the CLI to the cloud agent. It works in the background on a new branch and opens a draft pull request for your review. Autopilot works locally, and agent mode works in the editor while you watch.
Thursday morning Devin brought her a single line on a sticky note, which was new for Devin.

I'm asking before I do it. The drift script finds drift. I want the CLI to fix it too, every night at ten, before Kraków starts. copilot -p, fix any drift in staging, with --yolo, because nobody's going to sit up to press yes. That's the whole point of it.
Across the room Anders stopped typing.
In October he'd written the rule himself and posted it under his own name: nobody approves a command they haven't read.
A flag that skips the yes or no question. Staging. Nobody watching.
Devin wants a nightly CLI run that repairs staging drift with --yolo. What should Priya say?
A. Run it interactively at ten with someone on call to press yes.
B. Use --allow-all-tools with --deny-tool set for rm and git push.
C. Run it nightly with --yolo and rebuild staging if anything goes wrong.
D. Keep the night job to the script and have a person apply fixes by day.

The ten o'clock job stays the script, which changes nothing. When Kraków logs on, the report tells them which workspaces to leave alone. At 7:30 Devin opens a CLI session with the report attached, asks for a fix, reads the plan, and approves the apply himself. Anders comes over before they finish. In October I pressed Continue while I was on a call. That flag is the same button with nobody on the call. He adds one line to the draft of the team's CLI guide and puts his name after it: no allow all in any scheduled job.

That's how I'd chart it. Responsible use keeps a person on anything that changes state. A programmatic run can't stop to ask, so it shouldn't hold permission to make changes. Let automation report, and let people validate and apply.
Thursday at two Anders had a script for Joyce's list. He'd had the CLI write it in twenty minutes and had read it in twenty more.

What Anders's seat cleanup script does, in three steps. First a GET to the REST API's Copilot billing seats endpoint for the organization, which lists every seat, and then it keeps anyone whose last activity date is empty or more than 30 days old. Last, a DELETE to the billing selected users endpoint with those names, which puts those users' seats into pending cancellation.
Step two had found twenty eight people. Nora was reading the list over Priya's shoulder.
Anders's seat cleanup script is ready to remove everyone with no recent activity. What should Priya do?
A. Skip the API and remove the twenty eight from the GitHub organization.
B. Say go and remove the twenty eight seats Joyce's list asked for.
C. Run it for the empty ones only and keep anyone with any activity.
D. Go through the twenty eight names by hand before removing anyone.

They read the list together, one name at a time. Six of the twenty eight turned telemetry off in their editors, and the activity date only shows editor use when telemetry is on. Priya has watched some of them use Copilot this week. Two more people are on leave until January. Take those eight off the list, and that leaves twenty. Anders runs the removal Friday morning. Listed by the API, checked by people, removed Friday, Nora says. An auditor can follow that.

That's what I'd want on my shift. The seats endpoint shows each seat's last activity, but IDE activity only appears when telemetry is on. A seat list is where you start. Check it with people before you remove access, then remove through the API.
Decision ten. Still on the list.
Friday morning the removal ran for twenty people.
At eleven Nora brought her laptop over, open to the seat list from the API.
They're all still on here. Every one. The three I asked say Copilot still works. Did it fail? Finance reads this on the first.
Anders leaned in. Most of the removed names had a date beside them now. Four didn't.
After the API removal, Nora sees every removed user still on the API's list. What explains it?
A. They're pending until the billing cycle ends and will drop off in weeks.
B. The first call failed: the seats are live, and the job has to run again.
C. They're pending until the cycle ends, and four keep seats through a team.
D. It's a GitHub side bug that needs a support ticket filed today.

They read the API's response together. A removed seat goes to pending cancellation, with a date, and access ends when the billing cycle does. The four without a date get Copilot through the infra team's assignment, so removing them as users changed nothing. Two of them left infra in the summer and were never taken off the team. The other two moved to integrations in October. Ken takes all four off the team. Nora writes it down. So the list is right. It's just early.

That's the one I'd sign. Removing users through the REST API sets their seats to pending cancellation, and they keep access until the billing cycle ends. Someone who also gets a seat through a team keeps it until they leave the team or the team's seat is removed.
Friday at two Renata found out she was joining the infra rotation in December. She went straight to Anders.
I have two weeks to learn the infra folder. How did you learn it?
I wrote it. He looked at Priya's old runbook on the corner of her desk, the one with his name in the margins. More of the ask Anders lines had a stroke of her pen through them every week.
Then he turned to Priya. You're running this. How should she learn it?
A. Give her an autopilot session to make her first change on her own.
B. Have the CLI modernize the old modules, and then she learns the new ones.
C. Have her read the old runbook first, then use the CLI for what it skips.
D. Have the CLI explain each module and test it with terraform plan.

Renata starts in plan mode, which asks before it writes anything. She asks what each module does, which are still used, and what breaks if staging-db goes away. Then she runs terraform plan herself to see whether the answers hold. One doesn't: the CLI calls staging-db-old unused, and plan shows a backup job still pointing at it. By four she has seven questions for Anders, and none of them is where's the file. Those are the right questions. Those are the ones I can't put in a file.

That's how I'd chart it. Copilot speeds up learning a codebase and cuts context switching, because you ask about the code where you're working. Check what it says against the system itself, then bring a person the questions that need judgment.

At four she sent Joyce the list: twenty seats coming off, two people on leave keeping theirs, and six who'd turned telemetry off keeping theirs too. Joyce wrote back one line. That's what real looks like. Thank you.
At 5:10 on Friday Anders requested her review on a pull request: docs/cli.md, the team's guide to Copilot CLI, with a link to the Terraform instructions file at the top.
The first line said nobody approves a tool they haven't read. Under it, smaller: deny beats allow, so write the no first.
He came over before she'd opened it, and sat on the corner of the desk the way he used to when she was a data engineer and he was explaining something for the second time.
When I left in the spring, I gave you the platform and a runbook with all the hard parts missing. How many times did you write ask Anders in it?
That's twenty three things I should've written down and didn't. That was a bad handoff.
Not yet. Contracts end. Mine will. He tipped his chin at her monitor. Read it before you approve it. You've been the reviewer since October.

She read every line. She left one comment, on a sentence that said Copilot would ask before anything dangerous, and changed would to should. He accepted it from the corner of her desk without arguing, and she approved it.

Sunday was dinner in Aurora. Rice, measured to the first knuckle like always. Asha brought the cake from the bakery on Havana, the one she'd been calling worse every year since she moved down from Greeley.
Priya told them about the week. Forty one files, and a script that listed them before it deleted anything. Devin's ten o'clock job, and the flag that would have let it do anything it liked.

Her father put his fork down for the ten o'clock part. Second shift, the setup man wrote feed and speed on the sheet and went home. Your job was his numbers. Midnight, nobody around, foreman asleep in his truck. His numbers.
And if his numbers looked wrong?
Kill the spindle. Call him at home. He picked the fork back up. Earl. Hated the phone. Picked up every time, though, and never told one of us not to call.
Every standing order I ever followed had a phone number at the bottom, Asha said, and passed Priya the dal.

She caught every light on Colfax going home. In her own driveway, engine off, she opened the guide on her phone, scrolled past the last line Anders had written, and added one more. Then she typed her own name after it. If it looks wrong, stop it and call.
